text: Ludwig Prandtl (German pronunciation: [ˈluːtvɪç ˈpʁantl̩]; 4 February 1875 – 15 August 1953) was a German fluid dynamicist, physicist, and aerospace scientist who pioneered rigorous mathematical analyses in aerodynamics, forming the foundation of aeronautical engineering. In the 1920s, he developed the mathematical basis for subsonic aerodynamics, extending to transonic velocities, and established key theories including the boundary layer, thin-airfoil theory, and lifting-line theory. The Prandtl number is named after him. Born in Freising near Munich on 4 February 1875, Prandtl spent more time with his father, an engineering professor, who encouraged him to observe nature and reflect on his observations. He entered the Technische Hochschule Munich in 1894 and earned a Ph.D. under Professor August Foeppl in six years, with his thesis titled "On Tilting Phenomena, an Example of Unstable Elastic Equilibrium" (1900). After university, he worked at Maschinenfabrik Augsburg-Nürnberg, where he discovered that suction tubes failed due to flow separation, a phenomenon previously noted by Daniel Bernoulli, which led to his boundary-layer approach to fluid resistance. In 1901, he became a professor of fluid mechanics at the Technical School in Hannover, later the Technical University Hannover and University of Hannover, where he developed many of his most important theories. On August 8, 1904, he delivered a groundbreaking paper, "Über Flüssigkeitsbewegung bei sehr kleiner Reibung" (On the Motion of Fluids in Very Little Friction), at the Third International Mathematics Congress in Heidelberg, introducing the boundary layer and explaining flow separation and stall for the first time. The paper's impact was so significant that he succeeded Hans Lorenz as director of the Institute for Technical Physics at the University of Göttingen later that year. In 1907, during his time at Göttingen, he established the Motorluftschiffmodell-Versuchsanstalt (MVA), later renamed Aerodynamische Versuchsanstalt (AVA) in 1919, focused on wind tunnel measurements for airship models with minimal air resistance. During World War I, the facility conducted research on lift and drag on airfoils, bomb aerodynamics, and cavitation on submarine propeller blades. In 1925, the university spun off his research arm to form the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Flow Research, now the Max Planck Institute for Dynamics and Self-Organization. Due to the complexity of his 1904 boundary layer concept, its adoption was initially slow; only in 1908 did two of his students, Blasius and Boltze, publish dissertations on the boundary layer—Blasius on a flat plate in parallel flow and Boltze on spherical shapes—leading Prandtl to expand the theory to include a thermal boundary layer for heat transfer. By 1914, three more boundary layer papers were published by Göttingen researchers, but their dissemination remained limited until Theodore von Kármán published a 1921 paper on the momentum integral equation across the boundary layer. Following earlier work by Frederick Lanchester, Prandtl collaborated with Albert Betz and Max Munk on a mathematical tool for analyzing lift from real-world wings, resulting in the Lanchester–Prandtl wing theory, published in 1918–1919. He also developed a simplified thin-airfoil theory for cambered airfoils used in World War I aircraft and demonstrated that wing-tip effects are crucial, introducing the concept of induced drag and wingtip vortices, showing that an elliptical spanwise lift distribution minimizes induced drag. He later proposed a bell-like lift distribution that reduces tip loads by washing out wing tips to achieve minimum induced drag for a given structural weight, though this was initially ignored in aircraft design and has since been rediscovered and gained importance (see also the Prandtl-D experimental aircraft). In 1908, Prandtl and his student Theodor Meyer developed the first theories of supersonic shock waves and flow, including the Prandtl–Meyer expansion fans, enabling supersonic wind tunnel construction. In 1929, working with Adolf Busemann, he created a method for designing a supersonic nozzle, now used in all supersonic wind tunnels and rocket nozzles. His work on circulation was vital for ship propeller hydrodynamics, with most experimental work conducted at Göttingen from 1910 to 1918 with Albert Betz and Max Munk, and these discoveries remained secret from the West until after World War I. Prior to World War I, the Society of German Natural Scientists and Physicians (GDNÄ) was the only forum for applied mathematicians, physicists, and engineers in German-speaking countries. In 1920, they met in Bad Nauheim and concluded that a new umbrella organization for applied sciences was needed, leading to the formation of the German Physical Society (DGTP) that same year. In September 1921, the two societies met with the German Mathematical Society (DMV) in Jena, and in its first volume, ZAMM (Journal of Applied Mathematics and Mechanics) stated that this marked "for the first time, applied mathematics and mechanics coming to its own to a larger extent," highlighting the shared goals of Prandtl, von Kármán, Richard von Mises, and Hans Reissner. Prandtl and his peers co-founded GAMM (International Association of Applied Mathematics and Mechanics), which established a new international community of mathematicians, "scientific engineers," and physicists. Prandtl also contributed to the study of compressibility at high subsonic speeds through the Prandtl–Glauert correction, which became valuable during World War II as aircraft approached supersonic speeds. He worked on meteorology, plasticity, structural mechanics, and tribology. From 1921 to 1929, he investigated fluid instabilities, then shifted to developed turbulence, engaging in a competitive race with von Kármán to formulate a universal law of turbulence. Around 1930, both concluded that skin friction was inversely proportional to the square of the Reynolds number and logarithmically related to the product of Reynolds number and skin friction, resulting in a draw. Prandtl and von Kármán's boundary layer work was widely adopted by aerodynamic and hydrodynamic experts after World War I. In May 1932, the International Conference on Hydromechanical Problems of Ship Propulsion in Hamburg featured experiments by Günther Kempf that confirmed von Kármán and Prandtl's theoretical findings. After Hitler's rise and the establishment of the Third Reich, Prandtl continued as director of the Kaiser Wilhelm Society. The Nazi air ministry, led by Hermann Göring, used his international reputation to promote Germany's scientific agenda. Prandtl openly supported the regime, writing in 1937 to a NACA representative that Fascism in Italy and National Socialism in Germany represented "very good beginnings of new thinking and economics," and in letters to G. I. Taylor and his wife in 1938 and 1939, he stated that Germany's struggle against Jews was "necessary for its self-preservation" and that "if there will be war, the guilt to have caused it by political measures is this time unequivocally on the side of England." As a member of the German Physical Society (DPG), he helped Carl Ramsauer draft the DPG Petition in 1941, published in 1942, which argued that German physics was falling behind the United States due to the rejection of "Jewish Physics" (relativity and quantum theory), leading to a decline in the belief in "German Physics" superiority and allowing German students to study these fields in schools. Prandtl remained at Göttingen until his death on 15 August 1953. His work in fluid dynamics remains foundational in aerodynamics and chemical engineering, and he is often referred to as the father of modern aerodynamics. A crater named Prandtl is located on the far side of the Moon, and the Ludwig-Prandtl-Ring is awarded by Deutsche Gesellschaft für Luft- und Raumfahrt in his honor for outstanding contributions in aerospace engineering. In 1992, Prandtl was inducted into the International Air & Space Hall of Fame at the San Diego Air & Space Museum.
